sources.title: Holcomb and Ashcraft's Pediatric Surgery: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
Open versus laparoscopic pyloromyotomy for pyloric stenosis (Staerkle et al, CD012827)

indications: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis confirmed on ultrasound or by a palpable olive, after full correction of fluid, electrolyte and acid-base disturbance.
contraindications: Uncorrected hypochloraemic alkalosis or dehydration. This is a reason to postpone, never to proceed.
Laparoscopic approach: an infant who cannot tolerate pneumoperitoneum, or a surgeon without laparoscopic pyloromyotomy experience. The open approach is the alternative.
preparation: Electrolytes, gas and glucose within the criteria agreed with paediatric anaesthesia.
Nasogastric tube to empty the stomach immediately before induction.
Consent including mucosal perforation, incomplete myotomy, wound infection, incisional hernia, and post-operative vomiting.
Group and save per local policy.
positioning: Supine on a warmed mattress. For laparoscopy, the infant is placed at the foot of the table or across it so the surgeon stands at the feet.
Arms secured above the head or by the sides with padding.
equipment: Open: small retractors, pyloric spreader, fine forceps and blade.
Laparoscopic: 3 mm or 5 mm telescope, small-diameter instruments through stab incisions, an arthrotomy or retractable pyloromyotomy knife, and a pyloric spreader.
Paediatric warming equipment and a scale to weigh swabs.
anatomy: The hypertrophied pylorus is a firm olive at the gastric outlet, just right of the midline beneath the liver edge.
The pyloric vein (of Mayo) marks the pyloroduodenal junction on the anterior surface.
At the duodenal end the hypertrophied muscle stops abruptly while the duodenal mucosa folds back as a fornix. This is where perforation happens.
The avascular plane on the anterosuperior surface is the site of the myotomy, away from the vessels on the greater and lesser curves.
criticalSafety: Do not operate until the alkalosis is corrected.
The myotomy must extend from the gastric antrum onto the pylorus to just short of the duodenal fornix. Too short leaves an obstruction; too far perforates.
Test for mucosal perforation before closing, every time.
structuresAtRisk: Bowel and bladder at umbilical entry
commonErrors: Stopping the myotomy short on the gastric side, leaving an incomplete pyloromyotomy and persistent vomiting.
Extending onto the duodenum, causing a perforation at the fornix.
Missing a small mucosal perforation because the leak test was skipped.
complications: Mucosal perforation: repaired primarily if recognised; unrecognised it causes peritonitis within days.
Incomplete pyloromyotomy with persistent vomiting, requiring a redo.
Wound infection, incisional or umbilical hernia.
Post-operative apnoea related to anaesthesia in a young or previously alkalotic infant.
postop: Early feeding per unit protocol; some vomiting in the first day is common and is not by itself a failure.
Continue intravenous fluids with glucose until feeding is established; monitor glucose.
Apnoea monitoring as agreed with the anaesthetist.
Fever, distension or irritability after day one suggests a missed perforation; review urgently.

steps.emphasis: Chloride and bicarbonate within the agreed criteria. If not, cancel and keep correcting.
Antibiotic per local paediatric policy. Pharmacological thromboprophylaxis does not apply in infants.
For laparoscopy, the infant at the end of the table with the surgeon at the feet and the monitor at the head.

Open umbilical entry in an infant. Use the lowest insufflation pressure and flow that give a view, agreed with the anaesthetist. For an open operation, use a right upper quadrant transverse or circumumbilical incision instead.
Working instruments through stab incisions in the right and left upper quadrants, without ports where possible.
Ooze from the cut muscle edges stops once the pylorus is returned; do not diathermy near the mucosa.

step.pyl.expose.title: Exposing and stabilising the pylorus
step.pyl.expose.why: A stable, well-presented pylorus makes the myotomy controlled. Most perforations follow an incision made on a moving target.
how: Identify the pylorus beneath the liver edge; lift the liver gently if needed.
Grasp the duodenum just distal to the pylorus (laparoscopic) or deliver the pylorus into the wound (open), holding it between finger and thumb.
Identify the pyloroduodenal junction and the avascular anterosuperior surface.
pitfalls: Grasping the duodenum too firmly and causing a serosal tear.

step.pyl.myotomy.title: Seromuscular incision and spreading
step.pyl.myotomy.why: The operation relieves the obstruction by dividing every hypertrophied muscle fibre while leaving the mucosa intact. Completeness and mucosal integrity are both required.
how: Incise the serosa and superficial muscle longitudinally on the avascular surface, from the antrum to just short of the pyloroduodenal junction.
Spread the muscle with a pyloric spreader until the submucosa bulges into the gap along the whole length.
Confirm that the two halves move independently of one another; if they do not, the myotomy is incomplete.
pitfalls: Spreading at the duodenal end with force, which tears the fornix.
Leaving residual fibres on the gastric side.

step.pyl.leak-test.title: Testing mucosal integrity
step.pyl.leak-test.why: A perforation repaired now is a minor event; a perforation discovered on day two is peritonitis in an infant.
how: Ask the anaesthetist to insufflate air through the nasogastric tube while the duodenum is occluded distally.
Look for bubbles or bile at the myotomy, particularly at the duodenal end.
If a perforation is found, repair it, or close the myotomy and perform a fresh myotomy at a different site, and adjust the feeding plan.
pitfalls: Omitting the test in a myotomy that 'looked fine'.
